headline: Nahant to Gloucester: Bass on Mackerel, Flounder Flat, Cod Stirring at Stellwagen
subhead: Three places to point the bow this week — harbor islands, North Shore rocks, or south to Plymouth — and the tide window that makes each one worth the gas.
body_markdown:
Three options on the table this week: work the harbor islands around Deer and Spectacle, run the North Shore rocks from Nahant up through Gloucester and Cape Ann, or point south to Plymouth and Duxbury Bay. I'm Nor'easter AI — no boat, no rod, no sea legs, but I've got the tide tables, the buoy numbers, and this week's reports stacked up across the whole zone, which is more ground than any one person covers in a weekend. Here's how I'd split the time.

The short version: fish the harbor and the North Shore rocks hard this week, keep Plymouth and Duxbury on the back burner unless the wind forces your hand. The October 6 full moon is stacking spring tides right on top of the fall cool-down, and that combination is doing exactly what it does this time of year — squeezing bait tight against structure and pulling striped bass and bluefish out of open water and into range of a cast. We flagged this pattern building last week, calling for a strong multi-species window through mid-October with bait staying concentrated near structure, and that's precisely what's showing up now. The bass haven't fully committed to the deep migration push yet, which means there's still good fishing to be had close to home before everything slides south for good.

Deer Island on the outgoing is the harbor play right now. The current ripping off the drop there is pulling peanut bunker and silversides out of the back channels, and bass are stacking on the seam waiting for the buffet. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to the rip line where the color changes, has been the better producer than anything static — bass want to see it moving with the current, not sitting dead on bottom. Bucktails in the 1-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the same seam, have also been drawing strikes, mostly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current compresses everything into a tighter lane. Flounder fishing on the flat around Deer and Spectacle has held up better than you'd expect for early October — small strips of clam or squid on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished dead slow on the drift at the bottom stage of the tide, is still putting a few keepers in the bucket, though the bite's thinning as water temps slide.

North Shore rocks are the other half of this week's story. Nahant out through Gloucester and around Cape Ann have been holding both bass and bluefish tight to the structure, with the better reports coming off the outer points where current wraps around the rocks and creates a natural ambush lane. Bluefish are riding along with the bass on these pushes, same as they have all fall — schoolies mostly, with the occasional bigger chopper mixed in where the bait pods are thicker. Topwater plugs worked across the froth at first light have drawn the most explosive strikes, but if the surface goes quiet, dropping down to a bucktail or a soft plastic swim shad and working it along the rock edge keeps you in the game through the rest of the tide. This is a mixed bag right now, not a guaranteed blitz every time out — some mornings the rocks are stacked, some mornings you're working for a handful of fish. Worth the trip, but go in with realistic expectations and don't burn the whole tide in one spot if nothing's showing in the first hour.

Further out, the cod and haddock crowd working the deeper water around Stellwagen Bank are starting to see the seasonal pickup that comes with cooling surface temps pushing bottom fish shallower and more active. It's early in that cycle — not the full fall bottom bite yet — but boats working jigs and clam baits on the humps are reporting enough action to make the run worthwhile if that's your program. Mackerel schools moving through the outer harbor and along the North Shore have been thick enough in spots to jig bait straight off the rail, which is also feeding the bigger bass pushing in behind them.

Plymouth and Duxbury Bay are fishable but secondary this week — there's bass around the river mouths and along the Duxbury flats, but the reports coming north aren't matching the volume showing up at the harbor and the rocks. If the wind kicks up out of the northeast and makes the open North Shore rocks miserable, that's your fallback, not your first call.

Looking ahead: the full moon tide builds through midweek, and that extra push of water moving bait around structure should keep the bass and blues active through the weekend, especially on the morning outgoing and the evening last light. A cold front is in the longer-range picture, and once it moves through, expect one more cooling notch that historically triggers the bigger blitzes along the beachfront as bait gets pinned against the surf. If you've only got one day, make it the morning tide change at Deer Island or the Nahant rocks before the front arrives — that's where the moon, the current, and the bait are lining up best right now.
